500 MILLION

TWO-THIRDS
An octopus has roughly
five hundred million
neurons, but most of
them are not in its head.
They are in its arms.
How can an animal
think with its whole body?
In humans, most of
the thinking happens in
the central brain,
protected inside the skull.
In the octopus,
only about one-third of
the neurons sit in
the central brain,
which wraps around the
esophagus like a donut.
The other two-thirds are
spread through the eight
arms, where they work
as semi-autonomous
processing centers.
This means each arm
has its own local
nervous system that can
make simple decisions.
If an arm is
cut off, it does
not just go limp.
For a while,
it can still react
to touch, pull away
from harmful stimuli,
and even grasp objects
with its suckers.
Each of the hundreds
of suckers on an
arm is a tiny sensory organ.
They are packed with
receptors that can taste
chemicals by touch.
When an octopus reaches
into a dark crevice,
the arm explores,
tastes the surface,
and helps decide what
to grab, whether it
is a crab or
just a rock.
Scientists often describe
this as a partnership
between a manager and
skilled field workers.
The central brain gives
broad commands, such as
crawl toward that reef.
The arms then work
out much of the
fine detail of how
to move, without tangling.
Why did such a
strange system evolve?
Part of the story
may be the shell.
The ancestors of modern
octopuses gradually shrank
their shell, tucked it
inside the body,
and in octopuses lost
it almost entirely.
Without armor, an animal
becomes a soft,
protein-rich meal, so
octopuses leaned on speed,
camouflage, and clever
behavior.
Losing the shell also
turned the body into
a flexible canvas.
An octopus can squeeze
through any opening larger
than its beak,
the only large hard
part of its body.
Controlling a boneless
body takes a lot
of computing power,
and scientists think that
challenge may have helped
push the octopus nervous
system to become so
large and so unusual.
Our own intelligence grew
around a spine and
a single brain.
Cephalopods took a very
different road.
